fields.title: Watchman Nee (For Teens)
fields.description: Watchman Nee chose a name that called to mind a night watchman's clapper, the signal that wakes sleepers. He became one of China's best-known Christian teachers, the voice behind The Normal Christian Life and Sit, Walk, Stand, and spent almost twenty years in a Communist prison. This teen edition tells his story straight: the conversion that cost him his plans, the mentor who would not flatter him, the business controversy and six years of silence, the choice to go back to China, his 1952 arrest and the disputed charges against him, and the faith that was still standing at the end.

qa.question: Who was Watchman Nee?
qa.answer: A Chinese church leader and Bible teacher, born Ni Shuzu in 1903. Converted at seventeen, he founded a network of independent Chinese churches often called the Little Flock and taught messages later published as The Normal Christian Life and Sit, Walk, Stand. He was arrested in 1952 and died in state custody in 1972.

qa.question: Is the book honest about the hard parts?
qa.answer: Yes. It tells how Nee was shut out of ministry for about six years after a conflict over a pharmaceutical business, how he and his churches at first took part in public patriotic demonstrations and expressed support for parts of the new Communist government, and how the 1956 charges against him included sexual immorality. Where the sources disagree, it says so instead of choosing a side.

qa.question: What does “sit, walk, stand” mean?
qa.answer: It is Nee's summary of Paul's letter to the Ephesians. First sit: rest in what God has already done in Christ. Then walk: live it out in ordinary life. Then stand: hold your ground against evil from Christ's victory. The order matters, because you don't walk to earn a seat God has already given you.

qa.question: Was he put in prison just for being a Christian?
qa.answer: Not only that. The charges were political, economic and moral, and some are still disputed. But they came in a Communist campaign to bring independent religious leaders under control, and accounts report that release after his sentence ended depended on renouncing his faith, which he refused. That is why many Christians call him a martyr.

qa.question: How did he treat other Christians?
qa.answer: He refused to cut himself off from believers outside his own circle, which is why his fellowship with the Exclusive Brethren broke down, and he wanted ordinary believers, not only leaders, to pray, preach and serve. His movement later faced the charge of becoming exclusive itself, and he reportedly came to regret how often his wife Charity was left alone.

qa.question: Where do the stories come from?
qa.answer: From the full-length biography of Watchman Nee, which compares sympathetic movement accounts, recent academic scholarship, reference works, family memories and Communist-era records. Where they disagree, especially about the business conflict and the 1956 charges, it says so, and it marks family stories like his last statement of faith as remembered rather than word-for-word.

qa.question: What can a teenager today take from his story?
qa.answer: That faith can't be inherited secondhand; that you need people who will tell you the truth; that being right in an argument is not the same as being right in spirit; and that you are more than what you are useful for, because Christ is still enough when everything else is taken away.

qa.question: Why did he go back to mainland China in 1950?
qa.answer: He was in Hong Kong and had the chance to stay outside, and colleagues urged caution. He chose to return because he believed he should share the future of the Chinese churches. Two years later he was arrested, and he never lived as a free man again.

fields.title: The Sound of the Clapper
fields.body_html:
“Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel: therefore hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me.” — Ezekiel 3:17 (ASV)

Watchman Nee was not born with that name. He was born Ni Shuzu on 4 November 1903, in Shantou, in the southern Chinese province of Guangdong. His family's roots were in Fuzhou, in Fujian province. (Some older sources give a different year, and his gravestone has added to the confusion, but modern scholars generally use 1903.)

Years later, after he became a Christian, he took a new Chinese name, Ni Tuosheng. It called to mind the sound of a night watchman's clapper, the signal that woke people who were asleep. His English name, Watchman, carried the same picture into another language. A watchman doesn't make the sun come up. He stays awake while others sleep, watches for danger, and calls people to get ready. That is what Nee wanted his life to be.

He was born into a China in upheaval. The Qing dynasty, which had ruled for centuries, was close to collapse; in 1911 and 1912 a revolution overthrew it and set up a republic. For decades Western powers had forced their way into Chinese ports and politics through wars and unequal treaties. Missionaries had come too, building schools, hospitals and churches. Many of them served sacrificially, learned Chinese, and loved their neighbours. But because Christianity had arrived along roads opened by Western power, many Chinese people saw it as a foreign religion.

Nee's family belonged to the small Chinese Protestant community. His grandfather had served as a Christian minister, which made Nee a third-generation Christian, unusual in China at the time. His parents took part in church life. He went to mission schools, including Anglican schools in Fuzhou, and learned excellent English. Everyone who wrote about him noticed how bright he was: he read widely, learned fast, and had a remarkable memory. Before his conversion he was interested in political writing, and he had big plans for his future.

But here is the surprising part. He did not care much about the faith he had inherited. He knew the vocabulary. He knew the habits. He sat in Christian classrooms. None of that made him a disciple. Later this became one of the deepest lessons of his life: you cannot get faith secondhand. John's Gospel says God's children are born “not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.” A Christian grandfather can give you stories, prayers and an example. He cannot give you new birth.

John the Baptist warned religious people not to say “We have Abraham to our father,” as if having the right ancestors could replace turning to God. The same danger exists in Christian homes. A child can learn hymns before worshipping, doctrine before believing, and church manners before loving Christ. None of those gifts is bad. They are privileges. But a privilege is not the same thing as knowing God.

Maybe you grew up in church, or maybe you didn't. Either way, the question Nee had to face is yours too. Is your faith, or your doubt, actually yours, or is it just something you picked up from the people around you? There is nothing wrong with receiving faith from your family. Many people first meet Christ that way. But at some point what was borrowed has to become personal.

And notice the name he chose. Nee didn't call himself something grand. A watchman is ordinary, and easily forgotten. His job is simply to stay awake and to tell the truth when it matters. You don't need a platform to do that.

One thing to do this week: write down three things you believe about God. Next to each one, write where you got it: a parent, a church, a friend, the Bible, your own experience. Then pick one and ask yourself honestly, “Have I ever made this my own?” If the answer is no, talk to God about it, plainly, in your own words.

study_questions.question: What does the name Ni Tuosheng mean, and why did Nee choose it?
study_questions.answer: It called to mind the sound of a night watchman's clapper, the signal that wakes sleepers. He wanted to be someone who stays awake and calls people to be ready.

study_questions.question: Why was having a Christian grandfather not enough to make Nee a Christian?
study_questions.answer: Because faith cannot be inherited. A family can pass on stories, habits and an example, but new birth comes from God, not from family or effort.

study_questions.question: Why did many Chinese people of Nee's time see Christianity as foreign?
study_questions.answer: Because it arrived along channels opened by Western power, at the same time as wars, unequal treaties and foreign control of Chinese ports and politics.

fields.title: Not My Own
fields.body_html:
“ye are not your own; for ye were bought with a price: glorify God therefore in your body.” — 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 (ASV)

In 1920, when Nee was seventeen, a Chinese evangelist named Dora Yu came preaching. She was part of a wave of Chinese evangelists who were proving something important: the gospel in China no longer belonged only to foreign missionaries. Chinese Christians were preaching Christ to Chinese listeners, with real spiritual authority.

Nee's mother, Lin Heping, renewed her own faith under Dora Yu's preaching, and it changed the whole household. One well-known part of the family story is that she apologised to her son for having treated him unjustly. Later tellings may not have every detail exactly right. But think about what that would have meant to a seventeen-year-old: a parent saying, “I was wrong.” Seeing faith make an adult humble may have done more for him than any argument could.

Nee's problem was not that Christianity was strange to him. It was that he knew enough to see what real conversion would cost. He had ambitions, gifts and prospects. The gospel doesn't only ask whether you admire Jesus; it announces that Jesus is Lord. Nee understood that receiving Christ meant giving up the right to decide where his gifts and his future would go. That struggle was the heart of his conversion. When he surrendered, he described it as the beginning of a genuinely new life.

It got practical fast. Like many in the revival movements of his time, Nee set about putting right the wrongs he had done. Think of Zacchaeus in the Gospels, who didn't just feel bad about cheating people but paid them back. Making things right can't buy forgiveness; it is the fruit of grace, not the price of it. But grace that never changes how you live is worth questioning.

Then there was love. Nee cared for a young woman named Charity Chang before she shared his faith. He believed that marrying someone who did not believe would go against Scripture (“Be not unequally yoked with unbelievers”), and he faced a painful choice. He gave up the relationship rather than let romance rule over obedience. He had no idea how that story would turn out.

He later taught that surrender is not a deal with God. You don't give something up so that God owes you its return. Abraham raised the knife over Isaac without a secret contract. For Nee, as you'll see, the relationship did come back. Many faithful believers give things up that never come back, and their obedience is no less good.

And conversion turned straight into witness. Nee joined other young believers in sharing the gospel and studying the Bible. A huge ministry later grew from that small beginning: a converted student talking about Christ.

“Ye are not your own” can sound like a cage. But Paul never says it on its own. He adds, “for ye were bought with a price.” The One who claims you is the One who gave himself for you. Christian surrender isn't fear of a religious system; it is an answer to love. And it reaches into ordinary decisions: what you do with your mind, who you date, what you aim for.

One thing to do this week: is there a wrong you could put right? Something borrowed and never returned, a lie that needs correcting, an apology you owe? Pick one and deal with it this week, quietly and wisely. If putting it right might hurt someone else, ask a parent or pastor how to go about it first.

study_questions.question: What did Nee see as the real cost of becoming a Christian?
study_questions.answer: Giving up the right to run his own future. Jesus is Lord, so his gifts, ambitions and choices would belong to Christ.

study_questions.question: Why did Nee give up his relationship with Charity Chang at first?
study_questions.answer: She did not yet share his faith, and he believed marrying an unbeliever would go against Scripture. He chose obedience over romance without knowing how it would end.

study_questions.question: How is making things right different from paying for forgiveness?
study_questions.answer: Forgiveness is a free gift. Putting wrongs right, like Zacchaeus paying people back, is the fruit of grace, showing that it has really changed us.

fields.title: A Mentor Who Could Say No
fields.body_html:
“they that wait for Jehovah shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; they shall walk, and not faint.” — Isaiah 40:31 (ASV)

Near Fuzhou lived an English missionary named Margaret E. Barber. She wasn't famous. She had no big platform and built no big institution. She lived quietly, depending on God for her needs, and she prayed, counselled young believers and put good books into their hands. She became one of the most important people in Nee's life.

In 1921 Nee and his mother decided that the infant baptism they had received was not enough for them, and they were baptised as believers. Around this time Nee came under Barber's influence. He and other eager young workers would bring her reports of their activities and successes. Her replies could be searching. Had God started this work? Had they waited on him? Were they after visible success or after obedience?

Those questions sank deep. The biography puts the lesson this way: Christian work can be done for God without being done from God. Jesus said the Son “can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father doing.” If even the Son lived in dependence on the Father, Nee reasoned, Christian workers had no business acting on their own.

Barber also taught him to wait. For an energetic young man, waiting felt like wasted time. But a good idea is not automatically God's command for today. Some people stay extremely busy precisely because they are afraid to trust God. Waiting isn't laziness. It is refusing to let activity take the place of guidance.

Faith, he came to believe, is not the same as feeling confident. It is trusting the character of God. If you keep asking, “Do I have enough faith?” you may be looking at your faith instead of at God. Your security rests on how faithful he is, not on how strongly you manage to believe.

Her corrections could be severe. The point is not that she was always right. The point is that Nee learned to let his confidence be examined. Gifted young people especially need someone who is not impressed by their gifts. “Faithful are the wounds of a friend,” says Proverbs.

Barber also opened a library to him. Through her and others he read Andrew Murray, Jessie Penn-Lewis, D. M. Panton, Robert Govett, J. N. Darby, T. Austin-Sparks, George Muller, Hudson Taylor and many more. He soaked them up, adapted them and combined them in new ways. From Muller's story and others like it he learned to look to God for practical provision rather than make money the thing that decided his ministry. Later critics would ask how much of his teaching he borrowed. The fair answer, the biography says, is that he was neither a lone genius nor a mere copier, but a gifted interpreter who brought many streams together.

There is a question here for later. As Nee's own influence grew, did he keep people around him who could say no to him, the way Barber once had? The biography asks it gently, and it is worth asking of every strong leader.

Who in your life is allowed to tell you the truth? Not someone who flatters you, and not someone who tears you down, but someone who cares about you enough to say, “I'm not sure that's from God,” or, “You were wrong there.” If you have that person, they are a gift. If you don't, ask God for one.

One thing to do this week: ask one older person you trust, a parent, pastor, teacher or coach, this question: “Is there anything you see in me that I should work on?” Then listen without defending yourself. Thank them, even if it stings.

study_questions.question: What kind of questions did Margaret Barber ask Nee about his work?
study_questions.answer: Whether God had started it, whether he had waited on God, and whether he was after visible success or obedience.

study_questions.question: What does it mean to do Christian work “for God” but not “from God”?
study_questions.answer: To do good religious things in your own strength and on your own initiative, instead of depending on God and following his lead.

study_questions.question: Why do gifted young people especially need someone who can say no to them?
study_questions.answer: Because their talent can carry them a long way on its own, and people around them may be too impressed to correct them. Honest correction keeps them dependent on God.

fields.title: Right in the Argument
fields.body_html:
“who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:” — 1 Peter 2:23 (ASV)

In Fuzhou, Nee found friends who wanted the same thing he did: a simpler, more New Testament kind of church. With Leland Wang and other young believers, he met in homes to pray, study the Bible and break bread together every week. They preached in schools, in the streets, in homes, wherever they could, and a revival broke out among students in Fuzhou.

They were taking the book of Acts seriously. The first believers, it says, “continued stedfastly in the apostles' teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread and the prayers.” No elaborate machinery, no professionals performing while everyone else watched. Just people gathered around truth, shared life, the Lord's table and prayer.

Nee was still very young, but his mind, his urgency and his growing grip on the Bible made him a natural leader. And leadership exposed exactly the thing Barber had warned him about: himself.

Disagreements broke out among the workers in 1922 and 1923, over separating from the established denominations, over what the ministry should focus on, and over who should lead. Accounts differ on the details and on who was right. What is clear is that Nee went through painful conflict and was pushed out.

According to later testimony, when he went to Barber she did not take his side or tell him to fight for his rights. She pointed him to the way of the cross. That lesson became part of his vocabulary for life: you can be right in an argument and wrong in spirit. Winning can become an idol. A servant of God can have a real case and still be called to give up the need to come out on top.

Peter writes that when Christ was insulted, he didn't insult back, but “committed himself to him that judgeth righteously.” Jesus trusted his Father's judgment more than his own self-defence.

Now, this needs care, and the biography is careful. It does not mean that a person being abused should stay in danger. It doesn't forbid telling the truth, asking for help, appealing to someone in authority or getting protection. Paul defended himself in public and appealed to Roman law. The cross is not a tool for powerful people to silence anyone who criticises them. It means something narrower: your own rights can't become the most important thing in your life.

Nee came out of those early fights convinced that God cared more about what kind of person his servant was becoming than about whether the servant won. You can lose a position and keep Christ's character. You can also win the argument and lose it.

Jesus did answer his accusers sometimes, and Paul defended himself. So the real question isn't whether you may ever speak up. It's whether you can tell the truth clearly and still hand your reputation over to God, without needing to be proved right before you can have any peace.

Have you ever won an argument and lost a friend? Most of us know the feeling of being right and still being ugly about it: the extra comment, the screenshot sent round, the need for everyone to know you were right. Being right matters. But the way you are right matters too.

One thing to do this week: the next time you're in a disagreement, at home, online or with a friend, stop before you reply and ask yourself, “Do I want this sorted out, or do I just want to win?” Then say the true thing without the extra jab.

study_questions.question: What did the young believers in Fuzhou do together?
study_questions.answer: They met in homes to pray, study the Bible and break bread weekly, and they preached in schools, streets and homes, which helped spark a revival among students.

study_questions.question: What lesson did Barber press on Nee after he was pushed out?
study_questions.answer: The way of the cross: you can be right in an argument and wrong in spirit, and the need to be proved right can become an idol.

study_questions.question: What does this teaching NOT mean?
study_questions.answer: It doesn't mean a person being abused must stay in danger or keep quiet. Telling the truth, asking for help and seeking protection are still right.

fields.title: Racing Death
fields.body_html:
“So teach us to number our days, That we may get us a heart of wisdom.” — Psalm 90:12 (ASV)

In the mid-1920s, Nee became seriously ill with tuberculosis. He was in his early twenties, a young man who had expected decades of ministry, and suddenly he faced the real possibility that his life would be short.

He did not stop working. He threw himself into writing the material that became The Spiritual Man, a large and complicated book, partly because he feared he might not live to teach it any other way. You can feel the urgency in how dense it is.

The book's big idea is that a human being has three parts: spirit, soul and body. Nee built it on verses like Paul's prayer, “may your spirit and soul and body be preserved entire.” In his map, the body connects us to the physical world; the soul is the mind, the emotions and the will; and the spirit is the deepest part of us, where conscience lives and where we have fellowship with God.

Many readers have found this genuinely helpful. It names something real: not every strong feeling is the Holy Spirit, and a clever argument can come from pride rather than from God. Nee wanted Christians to ask not just whether something looks Christian, but where it comes from.

But the biography is honest that the map has limits. The Bible uses words like soul, spirit, heart and mind in overlapping ways. Mary sings, “My soul doth magnify the Lord, And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour,” and nothing in that suggests her soul was the problem. Jesus wept. Paul wrote with anguish and joy. Feelings and thinking are not the enemies of spiritual life. Treat Nee's scheme as a map, the biography says, not as the territory itself.

The illness also taught him something no book could. Paul once wrote about carrying “the sentence of death within ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God who raiseth the dead.” When your strength simply runs out, depending on God stops being a slogan. Accounts describe a remarkable recovery from the tuberculosis, and he prayed for it. But he never built a teaching that said faithful Christians won't get sick. The biography adds that health is a gift, healing can be sought, and medicine can be used.

There is one more thing here, and it matters for you. Nee wrote long before modern medicine and psychology understood things like anxiety, depression and trauma. Anxiety can make your body feel things that seem like spiritual warnings. Depression can flatten your emotions. None of that proves you are unspiritual. If your mind or your mood is struggling, that is not a failure of faith. Tell a safe person: a parent, a pastor, a teacher, a doctor, or a crisis line where you live. God often helps through people like that.

Nee didn't choose his illness, and neither do we. But mortality has a way of making you ask what you will do with the time you have. “Teach us to number our days,” says the psalm. That isn't gloomy. It's clarity.

Notice the order in Nee's life. Before he became a famous teacher, he was being taught. Before he wrote about resurrection life, he faced his own death. That is part of why his best teaching has weight: it had already been tested in a real body.

One thing to do this week: when a strong feeling hits you, name it honestly (“I'm anxious,” “I'm angry,” “I'm lonely”) and bring it to God in one plain sentence. Don't obey it blindly, and don't pretend it isn't there.

fields.title: The Church in the City
fields.body_html:
“Now ye are the body of Christ, and severally members thereof.” — 1 Corinthians 12:27 (ASV)

By 1928 Nee's work was centred in Shanghai, China's great coastal city of trade, printing presses and travellers. From there he published magazines and teaching that went where he couldn't, and a network of gatherings spread across the country.

Outsiders called them the “Little Flock” or “Assembly Hall.” The believers themselves didn't want a name at all. They wanted to be simply the church in their town, the way the New Testament speaks of “the church of God which is at Corinth.” Nee taught that all true believers in a city belong to one church, even if they meet in many places. The irony is obvious: a movement started partly to get rid of labels ended up with labels of its own.

Some of what Nee built was genuinely freeing. He rejected a strict split between clergy and ordinary Christians. In his gatherings, ordinary believers prayed, spoke, preached, cared for each other and carried responsibility. Leaders were there to equip, not to do all the ministry. A body where only one part moves, he said in effect, is a sick body.

He also wanted the Chinese churches to stand on their own feet: led by Chinese believers, supported by Chinese money, sending out their own workers. He was grateful for missionaries, but he believed that a church whose budget depends on a distant sponsor will end up obeying that sponsor. Nobody in the 1920s could see how much this would matter later, when foreign missionaries were forced out and public churches came under heavy pressure.

In 1930 Margaret Barber died. Some accounts say Nee received a large part of her library. Her influence went on through him.

In 1933 Nee travelled abroad and had contact with Brethren groups in Britain. For a while there was fellowship. But the relationship with the Exclusive Brethren broke down over whether he could share communion with Christians outside their circle. Nee refused to cut himself off from believers he saw as genuine members of Christ. For him the Lord's table said one thing above all: “we, who are many, are one bread, one body.”

The table did something else in his gatherings, too. Because the Lord himself was at the centre, nobody could make the meeting revolve around a preacher, not even a preacher as gifted as Nee. Rich and poor, educated and uneducated, leaders and brand-new believers all came the same way, as people who had received grace.

Here the biography is honest in both directions. Nee's protest against division was real and good. But his own movement later faced the same temptation he had just walked away from. A group that refuses denominational names and claims to stand on the one true ground in a city can quietly start treating other faithful Christians as second-class. Every renewal movement is in danger of becoming the thing it protested against.

Paul's answer to the Corinthians who were splitting into fan clubs (“I am of Paul; and I of Apollos”) was a question: “Is Christ divided?” Christians can disagree seriously and still treat one another as brothers and sisters.

Do you see other churches, or other youth groups, as competition? It is easy to. Nee's best instinct is a good test: if Christ has received someone, who are we to push them away?

One thing to do this week: pray by name for a church in your town that isn't yours. If you can, go with a friend to theirs once, and look for what Christ is doing there.

study_questions.question: Why did Nee's fellowship with the Exclusive Brethren break down?
study_questions.answer: They expected him to keep away from Christians outside their circle at the Lord's table, and he refused to cut off believers he saw as genuine members of Christ.

study_questions.question: What danger does the biography see in Nee's “one city, one church” idea?
study_questions.answer: That a group claiming to be the only true church in a city can end up treating other faithful Christians as second-class, becoming exclusive itself.

fields.title: Know, Reckon, Present
fields.body_html:
“Even so reckon ye also yourselves to be dead unto sin, but alive unto God in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 6:11 (ASV)

Remember Charity Chang? After she became a Christian, the door that Nee had closed opened again, and in 1934 they married. Even that wasn't simple. A relative who opposed the match attacked Nee's reputation in the press, and for a time he stepped back from visible leadership before going on with his ministry. Around these years Witness Lee became an important co-worker.

In 1937 full-scale war broke out between China and Japan, bringing enormous suffering, displacement and chaos. Nee's ministry carried on in a country at war. In 1938 he travelled in Europe and attended the Keswick Convention in Britain. Messages he gave during this period on Romans 5 to 8 were later gathered into the book known in English as The Normal Christian Life. He didn't sit down and write it as one book; it was put together from his talks. It became the most famous thing ever published under his name.

It answers a question many Christians quietly ask: if Christ has forgiven my sins, why do I still keep losing to them?

Nee's answer was that God has dealt with two problems, not one. The blood of Christ deals with our guilt, what we have done. The cross also deals with the old self, what we are. Paul says, “our old man was crucified with him.” God doesn't just forgive the old you and then tell it to try harder. He joins you to Christ.

Nee organised Romans 6 around three words. First, know: this has already happened in Christ, whether or not you feel it today. Second, reckon: count it as true. Nee liked a picture from banking. If money really has been paid into your account, you can count on it being there. Counting on money that was never deposited would be fantasy; refusing to count on money that really is there would be unbelief. Third, present: give yourself, your body, time, words and plans, to God, “as alive from the dead.”

He also loved Paul's cry in Romans 7: “Wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me out of the body of this death?” Notice, Nee said, it asks who, not what. The answer isn't a technique. It's a Person. And Paul's promise is plain: “sin shall not have dominion over you.” Sin may still tempt you. It no longer owns you.

He also summed up Paul's letter to the Ephesians in three words, in the little book Sit, Walk, Stand. First sit: rest in what God has done (Paul says God “made us to sit with him in the heavenly places”). Then walk: live it out. Then stand: hold your ground against evil. Get the order wrong and you'll walk to earn a seat you already have.

The biography adds an important warning. Counting yourself dead to sin does not mean pretending pain isn't real. Paul himself once wrote that “we despaired even of life.” You can be secure in Christ and still need counselling, sleep, a doctor or a hard conversation. Grace isn't threatened by help.

If you're stuck in the cycle of promising, failing, feeling guilty and promising again, Nee would say you're starting from the wrong place. You don't fight sin to become God's. You fight it because you already are.

One thing to do this week: write Romans 6:11 on a card or in your phone. The next time you fail, read it before you make any new promises. Then confess it, thank God that you still belong to him, and get up.

study_questions.answer: Know what God has done in joining you to Christ, count it as true the way you count on money really deposited, and give yourself to God as someone alive from the dead.

study_questions.question: What is the order of *Sit, Walk, Stand*, and why does it matter?
study_questions.answer: First rest in what God has done, then live it out, then stand against evil. Reversing it turns the Christian life into trying to earn what God has already given.

fields.title: Six Years of Silence
fields.body_html:
“that they might be with him, and that he might send them forth to preach” — Mark 3:14 (ASV)

This is the part of Nee's story that many short versions leave out. The full biography doesn't, and neither will this one.

In the early 1940s, with China at war and the economy collapsing, Nee became deeply involved in a pharmaceutical business connected with his brother. He seems to have meant it, at least in large part, as a way to support Christian workers through the economic crisis. It caused a major conflict in the Shanghai church.

The elders there opposed him. There were accusations and disagreements about the business, about his ministry, and about his personal conduct. The result was that Nee was shut out of public ministry for about six years.

What really happened? Here the sources split sharply. Earlier sympathetic biographies mostly tell it as sacrifice or misunderstanding. Hostile accounts present the allegations as settled fact. Modern scholarship treats it as a major turning point in his life, not a small misunderstanding. The full-length biography is careful: the evidence doesn't support a simple verdict either way. What is certain is that this period brought public humiliation, broken relationships, and a long interruption of his preaching. When you read about a disputed event like this, it helps to ask who is telling the story and why. A friendly source and a hostile source can describe the same years very differently.

Even without a verdict, there are lessons. One is about money. The New Testament doesn't forbid business: Paul made tents, and Lydia was a merchant. But when personal, family and church money get tangled together, people need to be able to see clearly what is going on. Good intentions don't remove the need for accountability. Trusting God is not an excuse for vague bookkeeping.

The other lesson is about who you are when your role is taken away. For a preacher, being kept out of the pulpit can feel like losing yourself. Many people only find out how much of their identity rests on being useful when usefulness is taken from them, through illness, a scandal, an injury or simply being replaced.

Mark's Gospel says Jesus chose the twelve “that they might be with him, and that he might send them forth to preach.” Being with him comes first. Being sent comes second. A season when your public role shrinks can still be full of God's work, because the first calling was never the role.

Maybe you've been dropped from a team, lost a part, been left out of a friend group, or had something you were known for taken away. It hurts, and it's okay to say so. But you were never just the thing you did. Before you were useful to anyone, you were loved.

And if you're ever trusted with other people's money, even the class fund, be the kind of person who keeps it clean and clear. It protects you as well as them.

One more thing. No Christian teacher perfectly lives out what he teaches, and the value of good teaching doesn't depend on pretending he did. The biography would rather tell you the truth about Nee than give you a statue. That's a kind of respect, both for him and for you.

One thing to do this week: spend ten minutes doing nothing “useful” with God: no list, no performance, no scrolling. Just sit, read a psalm, and tell him how you really are. If you handle anyone else's money, also write down every bit that came in and went out, and show it to someone.

study_questions.answer: Jesus called the disciples first to be with him and only then to be sent out. Belonging to Christ comes before any job or role.

fields.title: A Grain of Wheat
fields.body_html:
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a grain of wheat fall into the earth and die, it abideth by itself alone; but if it die, it beareth much fruit.” — John 12:24 (ASV)

In 1948, with Witness Lee and others playing a big part, Nee came back to public ministry. China's war with Japan had ended in 1945, but civil war had started again. And Nee's preaching had changed. Now it was full of brokenness, the church as one body, working together, authority, and giving everything to God.

The biography makes a point about any leader who is restored after a fall or a fight: he shouldn't come back unchanged. Restoration isn't just getting the platform back. Paul says those who restore someone should do it “in a spirit of gentleness; looking to thyself, lest thou also be tempted.” Nobody restores anyone from a position of superiority.

His best-known message from this time is about what he called “the breaking of the outer man.” The idea is simple to state. Christ lives in a believer, but the believer's natural self, the clever mind, the stubborn will, the self-protecting reactions, can block his life from coming through. Nee loved Jesus' picture of a grain of wheat. The life is inside the seed, but it stays alone until the hard shell breaks open in the ground.

He found the pattern all through Scripture. Jacob, the schemer, wrestled all night and walked away limping, with a new name. Peter swore he would never deny Jesus, then did it three times, and was restored afterwards: different, humbler, more useful. God doesn't throw away our gifts, Nee taught. He brings them through death and resurrection so that they become servants instead of masters.

Nee's own life had given this teaching weight. Gifted as he was, he had been contradicted, judged, sidelined and made to depend on others.

But the biography insists on a line here, and it matters for you. Brokenness language has been badly misused. Leaders have told people who ask questions that they are “unbroken.” Abusive groups have called humiliation “spiritual formation.” Victims have been told to put up with harm to learn submission. That is not what this means. God's breaking is never the destruction of your personality, the loss of your conscience, or obeying a human being no matter what. It never means accepting violence, sexual exploitation or lies in silence. No leader has the right to “break” another person. Jesus said that the rulers of this world “lord it over them,” and then, “it is not so among you.”

Nee's later teaching on spiritual authority needs the same guardrails. He believed rebellion against rightful authority can be rebellion against God. But authority in the church is always under Scripture, always accountable, and never an excuse for control.

In 1948 and 1949 the movement urged believers to “hand over” possessions for the gospel, and some families moved to new regions to plant churches. It was radical commitment. fields.title: He Went Back
fields.body_html:
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd layeth down his life for the sheep.” — John 10:11 (ASV)

On 1 October 1949, Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China. The Communist Party now held the state, and it set about remaking all of Chinese society. It didn't ban Christian worship overnight. Instead, religious life was reshaped step by step through campaigns, propaganda, patriotic organisations and growing control.

Protestant leaders were drawn into what became the Three-Self Patriotic Movement: self-governing, self-supporting, self-propagating, with all foreign ties cut. Here is the irony. Those words sounded almost exactly like what Nee had taught for decades. But the same words can serve different masters. For Nee, an independent Chinese church existed so that Christ, not foreign missions, would rule it. For the state, independence from foreigners was part of political control. The real question wasn't whether the church should be Chinese. It was who would be Lord. Words like “independence,” “unity” and “patriotism” are good words; what matters is how power uses them. Christians have to judge what is actually being done, not just the slogans.

In 1950 Nee went to Hong Kong. He had friends abroad and the chance to stay out of mainland China. Colleagues urged caution. He chose to go back, believing he should share the future of the Chinese churches. It may have been the most costly decision of his life.

The biography is careful not to say that every leader in danger must stay. Paul fled cities when persecution came, and Jesus told his disciples they could flee from one city to another. Scripture allows both staying and leaving, depending on calling. Nee believed staying was his.

But the story of those first years is not a simple tale of a hero resisting from day one. Recent scholarship notes that Nee and the Assembly Hall took part in public patriotic demonstrations and expressed support for parts of the new government, especially around the time of the Korean War. Chinese Christians were trying to survive in a world that was changing fast. Some hoped cooperation on national matters would protect freedom for spiritual work. Some genuinely welcomed parts of the new order. Some acted under pressure. Others, like Wang Mingdao, later refused the state-run church structures more openly.

Then came the denunciation campaigns. Church members were pressured to accuse their leaders in public and expose supposed crimes. For a movement built on trust, it was devastating. Nee's old pharmaceutical business now gave the state economic grounds to investigate him.

In April 1952, Nee was arrested, reportedly in Manchuria, on charges connected to business and political accusations. He was forty-eight years old. Nobody around him knew he would never live as a free man again.

Christians have two Bible passages to hold together here. “Let every soul be in subjection to the higher powers,” says Romans 13. Christians honour governments, even ones they didn't choose. But when the apostles were ordered to stop preaching, they said, “We must obey God rather than men.” Telling which situation you're in is one of the hardest things the church ever has to do.

Real heroes are usually more complicated than the posters. That's not bad news. It means God works through actual people.

One thing to do this week: pray for the leaders of your country by name, including the ones you disagree with. Then pray for Christians who live under governments that pressure them, that they would have wisdom to know when to cooperate and courage to know when they can't.

fields.title: How Long?
fields.body_html:
“How long, O Jehovah? wilt thou forget me for ever? How long wilt thou hide thy face from me?” — Psalm 13:1 (ASV)

After his arrest Nee waited years for a trial. The system did not work like a modern court, with a quick hearing, open evidence and an independent lawyer. Meanwhile the state pressed hard on the churches: co-workers were investigated, meetings were watched, and public accusation became part of the show. For the believers, the not-knowing may have been harder than a sentence.

In 1956 Nee was publicly condemned as the head of a “counterrevolutionary” group and sentenced to fifteen years in prison. The state's case included charges of economic misconduct, political crimes and sexual immorality. Many of the people who loved him were devastated.

How should anyone handle charges like that? The full-length biography refuses two easy answers. It won't erase the charges, and it won't repeat them as if they were proven.

On one side, the trial took place inside a system that used forced confessions and public denunciation as political tools. A confession signed under that kind of pressure isn't worthless, but it isn't like evidence given in a free court either. On the other side, some later biographers outside the movement argue that the evidence of serious personal wrongdoing was substantial, while accounts from within the movement stress fabrication, coercion and persecution. A Christian's loyalty to the truth means we can't declare every accusation impossible just because Nee was persecuted.

So the biography lands on something narrower and firmer. Nee was without question targeted and imprisoned as part of a Communist campaign to bring independent religious leaders under control. The exact truth of every moral and financial charge is still disputed. You can admire him without pretending to a certainty that history doesn't give.

His wife Charity paid too. She was educated and capable, and she also suffered arrest and persecution for being married to him. During his imprisonment she became one of his few links to ordinary life outside.

The churches went on without him. Some joined the state-recognised structures; some kept meeting outside them; persecution scattered others. Because ordinary believers had learned to pray, teach and gather in homes, the movement survived in many forms. The state silenced the teacher, but it couldn't easily silence the teaching.

What happens to your faith when someone you look up to is accused of something terrible? Paul gives a steadying line: “let God be found true, but every man a liar.” The truth of the gospel doesn't depend on any messenger being perfect. That cuts both ways. If a leader really did wrong, the truth should come out and be faced. If a leader is falsely accused, the truth should be defended. Either way, Christ, not the leader, is Lord.

The Bible itself doesn't airbrush its heroes. David committed serious sin and still wrote psalms we pray today. Peter denied Jesus and was restored. A faith that can survive the truth about people is stronger than a faith that needs its heroes to be perfect.

And if you are in a stretch of waiting yourself, the psalm at the top of this chapter is in the Bible for a reason. You are allowed to ask God, “How long?” Biblical faith makes room for that question, and God does not turn away from the people who ask it.

One thing to do this week: think of a Christian you admire, a leader, writer or musician. Thank God for what you've received through them. Then write one sentence finishing this: “My faith rests on Christ, not on them, because ...”

fields.title: Fifteen Became Twenty
fields.body_html:
“Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee the crown of life.” — Revelation 2:10 (ASV)

We know less about Nee's prison years than we'd like. Public records come from the state that held him. Family memories preserve precious fragments. Later devotional books sometimes filled the silence with stories that can't be checked. The honest thing is to say what we know and stop there.

His confinement included prison and “reform through labour.” Others controlled where he went, what he ate, the work he did, his medical care and his contact with family. Long imprisonment is mostly made of ordinary days: waking on command, eating what you're given, working, waiting for news, watching years go by. Crisis gives you adrenaline. Repetition asks for endurance.

Recent scholarship says Nee generally kept the prison rules while refusing to give up his faith in Christ. He wasn't a constant rebel. He cooperated where he could and drew the line at denying Christ.

Meanwhile something strange was happening. While Nee couldn't preach, his words were travelling. His messages were translated and published, and The Normal Christian Life found readers far beyond China. Paul wrote from prison, “I suffer hardship unto bonds, as a malefactor; but the word of God is not bound.” That doesn't make imprisonment good. Freedom is good and persecution is evil. But God can turn an attempt to silence someone into something else.

In 1966 Mao launched the Cultural Revolution. Churches were closed, believers humiliated, and religious leaders persecuted again. Charity and other members of Nee's family were interrogated and publicly humiliated too.

Nee's fifteen-year sentence should have ended in 1967. He was not released. Accounts commonly report that release depended on renouncing his faith, which he would not do. The exact details may not be right in every retelling, but the larger fact is certain: he was not freed, and he did not stop calling himself a Christian. “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick,” says Proverbs. He had taught about faith his whole life, and now the thing he surely wanted most, freedom, did not come. Faith remained when the answer was no.

His health declined, especially his heart. Letters with his family were limited and could be monitored. When she was allowed, Charity visited. There are reports that he came to regret how much of their married life she had spent alone while he travelled and ministered. We can't be sure of his exact words. If it's true, it shows a man still learning late lessons, and ministry is no excuse for neglecting the people closest to you.

We don't know what Nee felt every day. Faithful people in the Bible despaired, lamented and were afraid. Endurance doesn't mean feeling strong all the time. It means still belonging to Christ through the dark. Even Jesus, on the cross, cried out, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”

If you are in a long, dark stretch where hope feels sick, and especially if you've started to feel there's no point going on, please don't carry it alone. Tell a safe person this week: a parent, a pastor, a teacher, a doctor, or a crisis line where you live. That isn't weakness. It's one of the ways God holds people up.

One thing to do this week: send a message or a note to someone stuck in a long, hard season: sick, grieving, lonely, or far from home. Hebrews says, “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them.” Tell them you haven't forgotten them.

fields.title: Treasure in Clay
fields.body_html:
“But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves;” — 2 Corinthians 4:7 (ASV)

Charity died before her husband. The news reached Nee in confinement, and reports describe him as deeply grieved. Grief in prison is grief without any of the usual comforts: no funeral, no shared home, no long talks with family, no grave to visit. Paul says Christians “sorrow not, even as the rest, who have no hope.” Notice that he does not say they don't sorrow.

On 30 May 1972, Watchman Nee died in Anhui province, still in state custody, nearly twenty years after his arrest. He was sixty-eight. Accounts of his last hours differ; some say he died while being moved for medical care. There was no final sermon, no chance to revise his books, no chance to answer his critics or explain the disputed charges. History often denies us the ending we would write. The world outside had changed completely while he was inside: he died in the same year that the American president Richard Nixon made his historic visit to China.

His family preserved a short written statement of faith associated with his last days, reportedly found under his pillow. Different English versions circulate, so nobody should pretend to know every word. But its substance is clear: Jesus Christ is the Son of God, he died for sinners and rose again, and Nee died believing in him. It contains none of his famous vocabulary. Nothing about spirit and soul, or one church per city, or authority. At the end, the faith was simple.

Was he a martyr? Many Christians call him one, and the full-length biography understands why: he spent two decades in prison and would not give up Christ. It also notes that the charges against him were political and economic as well as religious, while the controlling context was the state's campaign against independent religious leadership. And it adds that being a martyr doesn't make every opinion or decision right.

His influence after 1972 was enormous. His books, many of them gathered from spoken messages, spread around the world and are read by Christians of many kinds. Witness Lee built an international network of local churches outside mainland China. Inside China, gatherings descended from the Little Flock carried on in registered and unregistered forms. They were one important strand, though not the only one, in the growth of China's house churches.

So what do we do with a man like this? The biography's answer is Paul's verse about treasure in clay jars. The treasure is Christ; the vessel is human and breakable. We don't need to pretend the vessel was flawless to value what God gave through it. And we shouldn't get so fascinated by the vessel that we forget the treasure. “Let no one glory in men,” Paul says. Thank God for what Nee saw, learn from what he suffered, question where his ideas outran Scripture, and don't build your identity on his name.

His deepest message is simpler than any system: stop trying to make Christianity work out of your own strength, and come back to Christ. He chose the name Watchman as a young man who wanted to wake sleeping Christians. Paul's call still sounds: “Awake, thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall shine upon thee.”

The watchman dies. Christ remains.

One thing to do this week: write your own short statement of faith, four lines at most, with no religious jargon. What do you actually believe about Jesus? Keep it somewhere you'll find it again, maybe inside the cover of your Bible, and read it on a hard day.

Witness Lee built an international network of local churches outside mainland China. Inside China, gatherings descended from the Little Flock carried on in registered and unregistered forms. They were one important strand, though not the only one, in the growth of China's house churches. So what do we do with a man like this? The biography's answer is Paul's verse about treasure in clay jars. The treasure is Christ; the vessel is human and breakable. We don't need to pretend the vessel was flawless to value what God gave through it. And we shouldn't get so fascinated by the vessel that we forget the treasure. “Let no one glory in men,” Paul says. Thank God for what Nee saw, learn from what he suffered, question where his ideas outran Scripture, and don't build your identity on his name. His deepest message is simpler than any system: stop trying to make Christianity work out of your own strength, and come back to Christ. He chose the name Watchman as a young man who wanted to wake sleeping Christians. Paul's call still sounds: “Awake, thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall shine upon thee.” The watchman dies. Christ remains. One thing to do this week: write your own short statement of faith, four lines at most, with no religious jargon. What do you actually believe about Jesus? Keep it somewhere you'll find it again, maybe inside the cover of your Bible, and read it on a hard day.
